story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Gilad.

dayfile.app is a "git log for scripts and agents", with ordered history, append-only logging as foundational characteristics. The service is currently in beta, AGPL-licensed.

As I was looking at various ways to record and retrieve a day's to-dos, automation and operational outputs (update successes and failures), the idea of a running event log. dayfile.app's primary use case is DevOps tracking and event logging. Building this, I've emphasized simplifying posting - one HTTP request with a title and optional tags (used for filtering when reading the log), AI access via MCP server (an assistant can read, post or close to-dos) and self-hosting as a first-class citizen (`pip install dayfile`, SQLite database is local in this mode).

A demo is available at https://dayfile.app/demo. If using the cloud service and after generating a write token on the site, an example of posting an entry would be:

  curl -X POST https://USERNAME.dayfile.cloud/events \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer WRITE_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Nightly backup finished","tags":["backup"]}'
To read back (filtering using tag):

  curl -H "Authorization: Bearer READ_TOKEN" \
  "https://USERNAME.dayfile.cloud/events?tag=backup&within=7d"
or paste https://USERNAME.dayfile.cloud/t/READ_TOKEN/f/backup.atom into a feed reader (you need to create a feed called `backup`).

What a local file can't do is notice something didn't happen - this is the heartbeat. dayfile.app can be configured to create an event if no associated event arrives. Imagine a backup which didn't run. A to-do event is created if no evidence of a successful backup shows up within a certain period. When the backup reports again, dayfile closes the associated to-do.

Current limits: logs are not end-to-end encrypted, sign-in is via GitHub only, the free beta allows 50,000 events and log size of 25MB. Pricing will be sorted out after this launch and as user feedback rolls in.

I'd love to hear in the comments on how you'd use it, what would prevent you from doing so, feature requests and suggestions. Bug reports can be submitted as issues on GitHub.

story_text.value:
I've been privately building a TypeScript SDK called TypeMaid and using it for my own projects over the past month.

It's based on Typed DAGs, with Mermaid diagrams to define and visualize AI workflows. I've found this approach surprisingly simple to understand and work with, especially compared to writing workflows entirely in code.

I recently open-sourced it and am now working on durability, retries, and persistent execution.

I'm curious what others think about using Mermaid to define executable AI workflows. Does this approach make sense, or am I missing something?

Would really appreciate any feedback, suggestions, or contributions! Star on github https://github.com/typemaid/typemaid

story_text.value:
I want to show you HippoMaps. It is a fully featured map and navigation app built on OpenStreetMap with a custom Overpass API engine for really fast search of POIs, areas and ways.

My aim with HippoMaps is to get to a level where I don't need Google Maps anymore. The biggest hurdle IMHO with OSM based apps is the lack of nice and fast search (where GMaps excels at). To get there I started working on a deterministic (as in no LLMs used) parser of queries that translates them to the Overpass QL.

Search queries are split into tokens and the algorithm tries to guess "what" you want to search and "where". The former comes from a word list (known brands, sports, OSM tags) and the latter from the geocoder service (Photon).

You can get quite creative like "cafes in Zurich by the Limmat", "peaks over 4000 m in Valais", "pharmacies open now in Bern". It's good for discovering hiking trails, e.g. "hiking trails from Arth-Goldau to Rigi Kulm". It knows how to find stuff between two places, next to a place, near a place and so on. You can stack those as well like "bridges over the danube in serbia 50 km from novi sad".

Except the search it has almost all of the features you would expect from a map like turn-by-turn navigation (Valhalla) with voice (Piper), public transport navigation in Europe (MOTIS), live traffic (only a few countries so far).

The app is GPL-3.0: https://github.com/cdutsov/hippomaps

I'm looking forward to feedback on searches that work or don't work for you + overall comments.

story_text.value:
I try to be a rational, rule-following actor.

Most recently hearing from industry professionals telling me they no longer read the code or care to understand anything that's shipped. I don't understand how a rational actor can assume "ownership" of a product and the associated blame if something goes wrong if the system under which they work requires them to ship at a pace which removes the capacity for diligence thereof.

The example being, if you ship AI code for 1 year and don't understand the codebase but are then triaged to on-call or something goes wrong, who is to blame? As a rational actor, you are operating in a system trying to keep your job and follow expectations but it seems that one aspect of your job (speed beyond human comprehension at the moment) contradicts the other aspect (tacit knowledge and deep understanding)

How do you participate in the games you see as strangely broken and absorbing massive tail risk [1], and how do you keep it from making you cynical?

[1] Tail risks that then seem to not matter in terms of enforcement, because nobody seems to be aware or care. I understand the other risk of existential death but balancing the two just feels tricky.

title.value: Ask HN: How to stay disciplined when tail-risk taking is rewarded?

story_text.value:
Hi HN! We're Tony, Kolom and Anastasiia, a small team from Ukraine.

Today we are open-sourcing Openspot, our research project on using generative UI in day-to-day work.

The idea is simple: generate a tool (spot) for your current task using coding agent, and keep it if you like it or remove it after use if you don't. We are using Openspot daily and really enjoying the possibilities it unlocks. Some examples of spots:

- caffeinate, which allows the Mac to work with the lid closed

- local file and screenshot search in natural language using EmbeddingGemma 2

- draw on screen during calls or before screenshots

- AI agents monitoring

- AirDrop, but over the network (using iroh)

We built it because of two things:

1. Over the past year, we (and almost every designer and engineer we know) have started making small tools using coding agents. But the DX for macOS applications is very frustrating even for coders, and you have to pay for a developer account to share them.

2. And we kind of miss the days of custom Winamp skins and Twitter clients. That's why every part of Openspot is customizable, so anyone can give it their own look and feel.

This is a very early stage. The code is MIT-licensed, and the core will remain free forever. We're sticking to macOS 26+ for now (because of Liquid Glass).

Ask us anything, or roast it. Any feedback is very appreciated.

story_text.value:
On November 18th, Google released another model, this one called Neon. Making it the fourth model in just 2 months.

OpenAI makes sense: Luna-Terra-Sol-Astra. Moon is smaller than earth, earth is smaller than sun and I can forgive them for not knowing that sun is also a star.

Anthropic is even better: Haiku-Sonnet-Opus-Mythos/Fable. Haiku is an extremely short poem, Sonnet is a bit longer, Opus is very long and Mythos is extremely long. Ok, Fable does not exactly really fit in there, but they came up with it after they only had the three models, so we had time to adjust. Also, Claude told me: Fable is basically Mythos with extra safety, and a fable is a story with a moral.

Now, I want you to think back to those high school chemistry classes. Which is bigger neon or carbon or hydrogen or argon? Impossible right? The correct answer, hydrogen, carbon, neon, argon, doesn't even match with model capabilities. To make things worse, there is no consistency, they are combining noble gases with other non-metals. You can't even say they went for easy names, helium, is not in there as an example. They really should have gone with just noble gasses: helium, neon, argon and xenon (skipping krypton to not confuse with kryptonite)

I'm glad that Google is sort of back in the race, but they should really invest in someone who is not AI-pilled to come up with these names.

PS don't get me started on Meta, wtf is a glimmer?

story_text.value:
Hey all! I ran into a wall with n8n - hard and expensive to scale, limited streaming, heavy MCP is confusing for agents.

That scaling was becoming more and more critical as I was beginning to build agentic swarms. So I built my own alternative with Elixir and Beam. Been using it in production for almost 2 months.

It connects my agent to multiple databases, sandboxes, and APIs. I've even migrated over my most used n8n workflows without a hiccup.

I ran some benchmarks and 10,000 concurrent workflows executed in 3 seconds and cost about 330MB of ram (listed as 512 in the case study). Equivalent workflows in n8n took 2GB of ram to run 100. It's roughly 200x the memory efficiency of the usual Node/Python stacks. And while you don't edit the workflows yourself visually, you can see and manage them through a UI, along with credentials that the agent never sees.

The workflows themselves are pure TOML. Not as easy as dragging node connectors. But the idea is that AI creates the flows and you can easily understand them.

This isn't a shaky demo. I'm using it as my daily driver to create complex multi-agent personas, run research and info gathering swarms, and whatever else my agent needs to get its job done. (it's built more than 70 so far)

I have a live working demo on my website that was built by an agent using Purple Flow to connect to my server. The demo itself lets an agent using Purple Flow access live (Adventure Works) data and generate reports, documents, and slides on demand. My agent and I built it in an afternoon. It runs on a lightweight model (to save money for a public demo) with very few hiccups.

- Repo: https://github.com/leetheguy/purple_flow - Discord, benchmarks, and demo links in the repo.

story_text.value:
OmnibusCloud aims to join different user devices into a single computing engine, which I call the Ultracomputer. Today it works with Windows, Linux, or Mac OS (ARM) computers. Next, it will be able to connect smartphones, tablets, game consoles, and any other computing device.

It is no secret that most of our computers spend most of their lives idle, and there have been attempts to use this idle power before. The most famous of them is BOINC. But OmnibusCloud, following the first part of its name, is trying to provide a system that will be easy to use for any actors.

OmnibusCloud is splitting tasks into chunks and distributing them to machines available to you. Each machine processes its own chunk individually and then sends back the result.

Today, OmnibusCloud is introducing simulation tools:

- ParaView plugin allows users to render engineering animations, similar to render farms like SheepIt does for Blender, on machines in your group

- PrePoMax solver replacement can distribute thermal analysis tasks to machines in your group

- WitSweep can plan and run hundreds of FEA (with CalculiX solver) or CFD (with OpenFOAM solver) cases in one click; you can schedule your research that will start on your office machines when everyone is at home, and then in the morning you will get the results.

OmnibusCloud works on a crowdcomputing model, similar to crowdfunding, but with computer power instead of money. The one who needs computation can open a project, and users can join it.

Today we are just launching the public beta, so there are very few users and machines, so to try our system, it will be better to start with a Private Group. Create your own group and invite your friends or team (or connect your office workstation) - you will get your own subnetwork to run your tasks.

Check our repositories: https://github.com/OmnibusCloud

You will find there public controllers and integrations with some applications (they are published with an MIT license) that you can use as an example to build your own controller or integration to solve your own tasks.

title.value: Show HN: Run CalculiX, OpenFOAM and ParaView jobs on your office's idle PCs

OmnibusCloud works on a crowdcomputing model, similar to crowdfunding, but with computer power instead of money. The one who needs computation can open a project, and users can join it.

Today we are just launching the public beta, so there are very few users and machines, so to try our system, it will be better to start with a Private Group. Create your own group and invite your friends or team (or connect your office workstation) - you will get your own subnetwork to run your tasks.

Check our repositories: https://github.com/OmnibusCloud

You will find there public controllers and integrations with some applications (they are published with an MIT license) that you can use as an example to build your own controller or integration to solve your own tasks.

story_text.value:
People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here.

It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work.

The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it.

I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email hello@foolscap.works I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome.

Thanks, David

story_text.value:
I've build whatislocalhost.com to showcase an app deployed to cloudish.ai -- Why?

Well, I can either buy ads and brain wash people or, I can burn time, tokens and effort creating value for the community, we chose the latter :)

The last year our team at Hal9 has been helping a bunch of founders that vibe-coded apps turn them into real MVPs (Minimum Viable Products) and then real products that scale in usage and revenue. One of the top questions we get was: why can't I just use my Claude Coded app as my website?

Well, technically you can, but as many of you in HN already know, not the best idea. Computers go to sleep, are more likely to get hacked with exposed ports, have slow and unreliable internet, you only have one, and if you are doing heavy work it will slowdown your website.

Therefore, I created https://whatislocalhost.com, which i an interactive explanation into what is localhost / 127.0.0.1 / ::1

Hope this is useful to some, or at least insightful.

story_text.value:
I have started using multiple models (Claude, Codex, Grok via cursor-agent, Z.ai, Deepseek, Hy4 via OpenCode, agy) etc, and I realized that I not able to identify which commit was made by which model. After looking around and not finding anything, I create a format specification that will let Model self-identify itself. The goal is a higher ranked model can verify the output of other models and suggest changes. It is similar how to a Senior Engineer will review the output of Junior Engineers. As Humans, we know which model is behaving well, and which we can trust more.

My AI based commits have a identification like this.

Add retry backoff to fetch

Model: claude-sonnet-5-5 harness=claude-code effort=high conf=medium

Model: opencode/hy4-flash-free harness=opencode effort=high conf=medium

In using this, I get an intuition what I can expect when I fire off model on a particular task.
